angle: Every Vampire cast is billed to all three seats: five entry converters turn each arriving body into table-wide damage (stack 009 prices one two-mana cast at exactly twelve per opponent), two death drains turn the table's wipe into your reach, and the commander runs the whole mint from a zone no removal spell can touch.

teases: One two-mana Vampire into three payoffs — and a pod at twelve is exactly dead (stack 009)
The wipe with your invoice stapled to it: how a dying board drains three seats
The end step that kills one opponent and leaves the other alive at exactly 1
Five-land hands the simulation keeps — and the Coach ships anyway

departments.headline: THE ZONE IS THE ENGINE
departments.dek: Your commander costs six mana, and the best thing he does costs none of it. Read the tax ladder before you decide Edgar Markov is worth casting at all.
departments.body:
Which card do you always have? Not the one you drew — the one in the command zone. CR 903.6 puts Edgar Markov there face up before anybody has a hand, and that guarantee is the only one this format hands you.

Eminence is why it matters here. It reads “Whenever you cast another Vampire spell, if Edgar is in the command zone or on the battlefield, create a 1/1 black Vampire creature token.” An ability that names the zones it functions in functions from those zones — CR 113.6b — and this one names the command zone out loud. Stack 002 has it firing from there, through two doublers, four tokens on one cast.

Two riders travel with it. The tokens are created, not cast, so they never trigger eminence a second time — the record closes that door. And casting Edgar is not casting another Vampire spell: he is the one Vampire in your deck that mints nothing.

Now price the man himself. Six, then eight, then ten, then twelve: CR 903.8 adds {2} for every previous cast from the zone, and the surcharge compounds for the rest of the game. The ladder beside this column is the whole argument for leaving him home. The simulation agrees: he is down by turn six in 52.1% of games, mean cast turn 6.6 — and the tokens have been arriving since turn one.

Colour identity is why the 99 looks the way it does. CR 903.4 reads mana symbols in the cost and in the rules text, so {3}{R}{W}{B} buys white's exile and board-wide protection, black's tutors and drains, and red's damage payoffs. It also shuts the door on blue counterspells and green ramp: this deck answers a permanent after it resolves, or it does not answer it.

Is the 21-damage clock real? CR 903.10a ends a player dealt 21 combat damage by one commander, and Edgar is a 4/4 with first strike and haste who puts a +1/+1 counter on every attacking Vampire, himself included. Treat it as a coincidence you can cash. Commander damage points at one seat; this deck's kill points at three.

One more zone fact, and it wins games against tax decks. Eminence is a triggered ability, not a cast. A tax on spells reaches the Vampire spell and never touches the token it mints.

★ Coach's read. The table re-prices you the moment your commander is read out loud, so stop buying anonymity you cannot afford. Spend the budget on order instead: land the two-mana payoffs while they still look like durdle, and let the six-drop arrive last, to a board he makes lethal rather than one he has to build.

★ And be honest about insurance. Your engine does not route through Edgar — eminence keeps minting whatever happens to him — so protecting him protects the wrong thing. What his presence buys is a discount: Flawless Maneuver costs {2}{W} while he waits in the zone and {0} the moment he is on the battlefield, and Deflecting Swat obeys the same clause.

captions.Flawless Maneuver: **THE ZONE SETS THE PRICE:** {2}{W} while Edgar waits in the command zone, {0} the moment he is on the battlefield. Casting him is also a discount on protecting everything else you own.

pilot_tips.text: Budget three mana for Deflecting Swat until Edgar is on the battlefield — the free mode reads 'if you control your commander,' and in half your games he is still home on turn six.

departments.pull_quote: Six mana buys the body. The engine came free, and it never left home.
departments.note: Commander File fast-facts and the tax ladder are rendered from goldfish + the card; body copy above supplies the CR teaching blocks (✓) and the two ★ coaching blocks.

departments.headline: EVERY CAST BILLS THREE SEATS
departments.dek: The table sees a six-mana commander and shields up for combat. You are not playing combat — you are casting cheap Vampires into a layer that charges every seat for each body that arrives.

callouts.title: LIGHT THE MINT
callouts.text: Cast cheap Vampires from turn one — twelve one-drops and seventeen two-drops keep the eminence tokens coming while the table watches someone else.

callouts.title: LAND THE CONVERTER
callouts.text: Impact Tremors, Corpse Knight, Witty Roastmaster, Warleader's Call or Purphoros — one of the five is in hand by turn six in 62.6% of games, and from that moment every body is damage at three seats.

callouts.title: STACK THE MULTIPLIERS
callouts.text: Anointed Procession and Mondrak double every mint — stack 002 turns one two-mana cast into five bodies, and stack 009 turns the same shape into twelve damage per opponent.

callouts.title: WELCOME THE WIPE
callouts.text: Blood Artist and Cruel Celebrant drain as the board dies, and eminence rebuilds from a zone no sweeper touches. Commit in waves and get paid both directions.

captions.Impact Tremors: **THE TWO-MANA KILL LAYER:** every creature you get, each opponent pays one. It reads as durdle on turn two, which is exactly why it survives to matter.
captions.Cordial Vampire: **THE SPARK OF STACK 009:** the two-mana cast that set off nine triggers and killed a pod at twelve. Any cheap Vampire in your hand is this card waiting for the right board.
captions.Blood Artist: **THE INVOICE ON THE WIPE:** one drain per death, aimed where you choose. The sweeper the table is holding pays you on resolution — point him at whoever cast it.

pilot_tips.text: Feed Skullclamp eminence tokens, never lords — a 1/1 dies to the toughness change and pays two cards, every single time.

departments.pull_quote: They shielded up for combat. The kill never declared an attacker.

departments.headline: SIXTY-THREE SPELLS, ONE EVENT
departments.dek: Sorted by what each card does when a creature enters the battlefield, because that is the moment this deck is built around. The five converters lead; almost everything else exists to feed them.

roster.role: The conversion layer: every entry is damage
The multipliers: one token becomes four
The death drains: the wipe pays you
The deterministic kill, and the rent it pays
cards: Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose
Legion's Landing // Adanto, the First Fort

roster.role: Lords, anthems, and the counters that travel
Cheap Vampires that feed the mint
Interaction, and insurance sized for a board

cards: Midgar, City of Mako // Reactor Raid

captions.Witty Roastmaster: **CONVERTER NUMBER FIVE:** not a Vampire, and the deck does not care — it converts entries, and eminence supplies the entries. Five copies of this effect is what makes the kill a plan instead of a draw.
captions.Pact of the Serpent: **THE WIDTH-PRICED REFILL:** name Vampire, draw a card per body, pay the same in life — a currency the drains rebate. Cast it after the mint, never before.
captions.Sanguine Bond: **HALF A LOOP AT ALL TIMES:** with Bloodthirsty Conqueror it is stack 006's table-kill; alone it turns every Sanctum Seeker attack into a second bill for one opponent.

pilot_tips.text: Fire Olivia's Wrath at an opponent's board, never to tidy your own — five of your 29 creatures are not Vampires, and two of them are converters.

departments.pull_quote: Rank matters: the load-bearing cards are the five that make a body cost the table something.

departments.headline: MULLIGAN LIKE HE ISN'T THERE
departments.dek: You just read the distribution — twelve one-drops, seventeen two-drops, 37 lands. Now grade four openers against it, because the simulation keeps 80.8% of first sevens and the Coach ships one of them anyway.

hands.why: Three lands that can all arrive untapped, two one-mana Vampires worth two bodies each, a lord, and the two-mana payoff that turns the whole thing into damage. Something to cast on turns one, two and three, and a converter behind it — this is the shape the drill is looking for.

Two lands reads risky until you price the mana. Ancient Tomb into Sol Ring is three available on turn one against a simulated mean of 1.0, and Herald's Horn rebates {1} off every Vampire behind it. Both lands enter untapped, and that is the detail that saves the keep.

Half a deterministic kill and four five-drops. Two of these lands enter tapped no matter what, nothing happens before turn five, and your eminence dividend for four whole turns is zero. Ship any hand whose cheapest spell costs five.

hands.verdict: SHIP — the hand the machine keeps
hands.why: The simulation's rule keeps any seven holding two to five lands, so this five-lander passes — and the Coach ships it anyway. One castable spell before turn four, and protection plus a tutor are luxuries in an opener, not a plan. The badges disagreeing in public is the honest version of this section.

captions.Concealed Courtyard: **THE FIRST-THREE-TURNS LAND:** untapped exactly while twelve one-drops and seventeen two-drops need it. Fifteen of the 37 lands can enter tapped; only three always do.
captions.Ancient Tomb: **TWO MANA FOR TWO LIFE:** the fastest land here, and your speed is worth the life. It is what turns a two-lander into a turn-two three-drop.
captions.Herald's Horn: **THE MARGINAL-HAND FIXER:** {1} off every Vampire spell and a free look at the top each upkeep. Ramp or fixing shows up in 68.0% of games at a mean turn of 3.0.

pilot_tips.text: Grade a one-drop by casts, not stats — Vampire of the Dire Moon on turn one is a deathtouch blocker plus a banked eminence token before it does anything else.

departments.pull_quote: He is face up in the command zone before your first decision. Mulligan as though he does not exist.

departments.headline: TWO BOARDS, ONE HABIT
departments.dek: Turn six with six mana and a commander in the zone; turn seven with a sweeper telegraphed and lethal one cast away. Commit to a line on each before the Coach shows his — both answers come down to counting triggers instead of fearing them.

callouts.title: COUNT THE TRIGGERS FIRST
callouts.text: Before you weigh any line, total what each cast actually bills the table through the converters and doublers already down. The flashy play and the correct play are rarely the same size.

callouts.title: THEN PRICE THE WRATH
callouts.text: A control seat passing with four or more untapped lands is holding a sweeper — assume it, then ask what it costs THEM to cast it into your drains before you decide what it costs you.

pilot_tips.text: Hold Teferi's Protection for the turn you go all-in, not the turn after — protection is in hand by turn six in only half your games, so when you have it, spend it on the commit.

departments.pull_quote: Commit first. The Coach shows his hand only after you have shown yours.
departments.note: Two decision spreads render from decisions/001 and 002. Neither headline nor furniture may telegraph a recommendation (L1); the callouts teach the method, not the answer.

departments.headline: TWELVE TO EVERY SEAT
departments.dek: Seven lines, argued and affirmed — from the token math underneath everything to the two-mana cast that killed a pod exactly. Including the one line the record stopped short of calling a kill, because honesty is the house style.

callouts.title: THE MINT
callouts.text: Stack 002: one {B}{B} Vampire spell through Anointed Procession and Mondrak is five bodies — 1 becomes 2 becomes 4 in an order you choose, and the result is identical either way. The tokens are created, not cast: no second eminence trigger, no loop.

callouts.title: THE CONVERSION
callouts.text: Stack 008: the same cast with Purphoros watching is five entry triggers at 2 damage each — 10 to every opponent. Stack 009 composes three payoffs on one cast: nine triggers, twelve per seat, exactly lethal to a pod at twelve. Zero margin, zero combat.

callouts.title: THE ATTACK
callouts.text: Stack 003: seven attacking Vampires under Sanctum Seeker and Bloodletter drain each opponent 14 at declare-attackers — the seat at 14 is dead before a blocker exists.

callouts.title: THE LOOP
callouts.text: Stacks 004 and 006: Bloodthirsty Conqueror with Vito or Sanguine Bond converts any life gain into a chain that walks the table one seat at a time. Both checker-passed; both rest on one 5/5 the table can kill at instant speed, and every iteration passes priority.

callouts.title: THE BOUNDARY
callouts.text: Stack 007, the fun one: Throne of the God-Pharaoh under Bloodletter drains each opponent 14 at your end step — kills the seat at 9, and leaves the seat at 15 alive at exactly 1. Partially refuted as a table-kill, and the record says so out loud.

captions.Cordial Vampire: **THE TWO-MANA TRIGGER STORM:** stack 009's cast. Three entry events, nine triggers, twelve damage per opponent — and the win arrives as one simultaneous state-based check.
captions.Purphoros, God of the Forge: **NOT A CREATURE, STILL LETHAL:** devotion three keeps him an inanimate god in stack 009, and it costs him nothing — a permanent's abilities work from the battlefield regardless of card type.
captions.Throne of the God-Pharaoh: **THE HONEST ONE:** fourteen per seat at your end step is enormous and still not a table-kill — one opponent lives at exactly 1. Know your line's ceiling before you bet the turn on it.

departments.pull_quote: Exactly lethal, zero margin — the record's favourite kind of arithmetic.
departments.note: Feature order: 009 leads (the primary plan as rules-fact), then 008, 003, 004, 006, 007, with 002 as the foundation box. Only presentable checker-passed stacks appear; full citations live in Judge's Desk.

departments.headline: LET THEM UNDERPRICE YOU
departments.dek: The table sees an empty command zone and prices a deck that starts on turn six. Yours started on turn one — here is when they notice, and what to do before and after that moment.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: You flip to archenemy the moment a converter is on the battlefield next to a doubler — that is when the table stops seeing chump blockers and starts doing the entry math. Land the pieces while they read as durdle; after the flip, every untapped mana at the table is aimed at you.

captions.Anointed Procession: **VISIBLY DOES NOTHING THE TURN IT RESOLVES:** which is exactly why it survives. Slide it in behind the cheap bodies, before the loud turn.
captions.Elspeth, Storm Slayer: **ATTACKED ON SIGHT:** a planeswalker doubling tokens draws every eye at the table. She comes down last, to a board that protects her — never first.

pilot_tips.text: Point Blood Artist at whoever cast the wipe — the drain chooses its target per death, and the invoice lands hardest on the seat that thought the wrath was an exit.

departments.pull_quote: The clock the table cannot see: two bodies by turn three, 4.2 by turn six, off cards that look like draft commons.

departments.headline: WHO ACTUALLY BEATS YOU
departments.dek: Not the sweeper — you charge admission for that. The seats to respect are the lock that stops creatures entering, the combo clock you cannot counter, and the graveyard you answer with tempo instead of cards.

threats.read: The 99 holds no stack interaction, so the only lever is the clock: the kill config is assembled by turn six in 41.7% of games, 57.7% when a tutor buys the missing half. Spend Demonic Tutor and Vampiric Tutor on the kill, mark the combo seat as the converters' first target, and when you present lethal, count the table's open mana and assume every held answer appears. Prefer the triggers-plus-attack kill that leaves a board behind over the Conqueror loop that rests on one 5/5.

The tax half is survivable — eminence is a triggered ability from the command zone, so a spell tax reaches the Vampire spell and never the token, and 29 of your 63 spells cost two or less. The piece that actually beats you stops creatures from entering or shuts off life loss. Name it, then spend the matching answer: Despark starts at mana value four, so the cheap piece takes Generous Gift or Stroke of Midnight, and Anguished Unmaking is reserved for the one you cannot see resolve twice.

The wrath is a worse card against you than against anyone else at the table. The converters, doublers and rebates are mostly enchantments and artifacts that stand through it, Purphoros is indestructible, eminence rebuilds from an untouchable zone — and with a death drain down, the wipe itself bills every seat as your board leaves. Protection is in hand by turn six in only 50.0% of games; in the other half, the drains ARE the policy. Commit in waves and keep the best threat in hand for their second sweeper.

Re-ask the role per seat: against a faster board you are the control without changing a card. Deathtouch and lifelink make attacking you a losing trade, first strike wins the even fights, and every drain raises your total while lowering theirs — their damage-per-card rate drops below lethal while yours never routes through combat at all. Sanctum Seeker is the mirror-breaker: stack 003 prices seven attackers at 14 off each opponent before blockers.

The honest box: you hold zero graveyard answers — confirmed down to the oracle text — so this seat is answered by clock, not cards. Mark them the priority target early and aim the converter damage there. The consolation runs the other way too: this 99 puts nothing in its own yard on purpose, so their graveyard hate exiles air. The one card to respect is an exile-instead effect, which mutes the death drains — shift the kill onto the entry converters and Sanctum Seeker, which never cared.

pilot_tips.text: Save Winds of Abandon for the one board wider than yours — overloaded it exiles every creature you do not control, and your tokens stay to swing into the ramp they were handed.

departments.pull_quote: Their graveyard hate exiles air. Smile and say thank you.

departments.headline: BUY THE KILL, NOT THE LOOP
departments.dek: Cast a black tutor and three seats decide you are digging for the infinite. You almost never are: sixteen points of your turn-six kill rate live in these three cards, and they belong to the converter layer.

captions.Demonic Tutor: **THE WORKHORSE:** two mana, any card, to hand — the only wish you cash the same turn. Plan it as Tutor plus a two-drop on turn four.
captions.Vampiric Tutor: **THE END-STEP WISH:** one mana at instant speed, card on top, two life. Cast it when the table's mana is spent, cash it the turn it arrives.
captions.Diabolic Intent: **THE SACRIFICE IS FREE:** eminence prints the currency — cast a Vampire first and pay the Intent with the token it minted.

pilot_tips.text: Never tutor Bloodletter onto a board that cannot pay {B}{B}{B} on schedule — it is the only triple-black cast in the 99, in your thinnest colour.

departments.pull_quote: The loop assembles in 4.8% of your games on natural draws. Carry the ticket; never steer for it.
departments.note: Entries render from tutor_guide.json — the kicker/dek frame Sunny's assessment: kill config 41.7% by turn six on natural draws, 57.7% tutor-assisted; the loop 4.8% unassisted, 24.3% with tutors.

departments.headline: BLACK RUNS THE INVOICE
departments.dek: Half the deck's coloured demand is black — 51.3% of the pips on 42.9% of the sources — and the drain payoffs are the black cards. Here is what that gap costs, measured, and what the other two colours got instead.

captions.Cavern of Souls: **THE FINE PRINT:** its coloured mana casts creature spells only — it cannot pay Castle Locthwain's draw, Bloodline Keeper's flip, or any activated cost. It accelerates the tribe without powering the machinery.
captions.City of Brass: **A LIFE PER TAP FOR PERFECT FIXING:** in a deck that banked seven life across one verified attack (stack 003), that is the cheapest fixing money can buy.

pilot_tips.text: Tap Talisman for the black pip, not the red — 39 of the deck's 76 coloured pips are black and only 27 sources pay them.

departments.pull_quote: Ninety percent is a yardstick. Thirty-seven lands is a decision.
departments.note: Tables and meters render from mana_analysis.json; body prose is the writer's mana_base key. Ledger's frame: W 89.5% / R 83.1% / B 76.4% on-curve with rocks, 15 of 37 lands can enter tapped but only three always do.

departments.headline: THE MACHINE, MEASURED
departments.dek: Seeded, rerunnable, and honest about what it is not: a resource-development model, not a game. What it says is that the engine shows up on time and the commander does not — which is the design working.

callouts.title: THE KEEP
callouts.text: 80.8% of first sevens are keepable, mean mulligans 0.227 — the drill in Keep or Ship is about spotting the bad fifth hand, not agonizing over every seven.

callouts.title: THE CURVE HOLDS
callouts.text: 91.9% hit the turn-3 land drop and mean available mana is 5.3 by turn six — enough for every spell in a deck whose curve tops at six and modes at three.

callouts.title: THE KILL CONFIG
callouts.text: A converter and a multiplier are both drawn by turn six in 41.7% of games — 57.7% when a tutor buys the missing half. That sixteen-point spread is the whole argument of Fetch Quests.

callouts.title: THE COMMANDER IS LATE, ON PURPOSE
callouts.text: Edgar's mean cast turn is 6.6 and he is down by turn six in 52.1% of games — while a converter arrives at a mean turn of 2.8. The deck's opening act never waits for its headliner.

captions.Champion of Dusk: **THE REFILL, PRICED IN LIFE:** a draw engine is drawn in 73.4% of games, 62.2% by turn six — this one pays cards-per-Vampire in a currency the drains rebate.

departments.pull_quote: The infinite assembles unassisted in 4.8% of games. The deck wins the other way, and the numbers know it.
departments.note: Stated-assumptions box is non-negotiable: the goldfish models resource development, not games, and every figure above is quoted exactly from goldfish_metrics.json (seed 42, 10,000 iterations).

departments.headline: TEN CARDS, TWO NUMBERS
departments.dek: Twenty-seven and zero: black sources against a 36-source yardstick, and answers to a graveyard. Three of the ten move the first number, one closes the second, and the rest deepen an engine that already works.

callouts.title: THE PLUMBING
callouts.text: Path of Ancestry and Isolated Chapel each add a black source without costing white or red; Soul-Guide Lantern closes the one uncovered interaction class for a single colourless mana. Plumbing is where a marginal dollar buys the most.

callouts.title: THE ENGINE DEPTH
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood is the headline: with Vito, Sanguine Bond and Bloodthirsty Conqueror all in the 99, one enchantment turns two loop pairings into four — a second copy of a proven engine, not a new one.

callouts.title: THE FAMOUS ABSENCE
callouts.text: Rest in Peace would cover the graveyard for two mana — and under it your creatures exile instead of dying, blanking Blood Artist, Cruel Celebrant and Cordial Vampire. The Lantern does the job without the friendly fire.

departments.pull_quote: Not a shopping list — a watch list priced in advance: what it closes, what it unlocks, what it would replace.
departments.note: Exactly ten entries render from considering.json; deltas are ◆, recommendations are ★, and lines the list would open stay candidates until a stack passes.

departments.headline: SEVEN CASES, READ TWICE
departments.dek: Every citation verbatim, every verdict on the record — including the line that fell one life short of a table-kill. This department is the reason to believe the other sixteen.
departments.pull_quote: Where the record is silent, so am I.
departments.note: Rendered verbatim from the seven presentable checker-passed stacks (002, 003, 004, 006, 007, 008, 009). No summarizing, no truncation.

departments.headline: SEVENTY-EIGHT HANDS
departments.dek: Seventy-eight artists split 97 cards, sixty-one of them appear exactly once, and the census leader holds four — three of them landscapes. Nobody painted this deck; that is the story.

featured.note:
Four cards of 97, and three are places: Castle Locthwain, Luxury Suite and Savai Triome. The fourth is Throne of the God-Pharaoh — the card the record bounded, in stack 007: fourteen out of each seat at your end step, one opponent dead, the other alive at exactly 1.

Four of 97 is a 4.1% share and we are not calling it dominance; the runner-up holds two. The analysis found no collector-number runs anywhere in the deck — no product bought whole — and Lunter's four span three sets across three years. This 99 was assembled a card at a time, and a credits page with seventy-eight names on it is exactly what that looks like.

So the feature goes to the deck's scenery painter: the artist whose job here is the ground the Vampires stand on, plus one golden throne that turned out to have a body count.

also_worth_noting.note: Two cards: Edgar Markov and Sanctum Seeker — the commander and the drain that prices his attacks. Stack 003 runs seven Vampires through that Seeker for 14 off each opponent before a blocker exists. One painter, one verified kill.
Two cards that want the same turn: Bloodletter of Aclazotz doubles what each opponent loses, and Akroma's Will picks the mode nobody at the table can answer.
Purphoros, God of the Forge and Captivating Vampire — the biggest converter in the deck, and the lord that taps five Vampires to take something of yours.
Blood Crypt and Silent Clearing, both night scenes — the closest this deck comes to a mood board.
Two lands doing quiet jobs: Cavern of Souls, which makes your Vampire spells uncounterable, and Reflecting Pool.

captions.Throne of the God-Pharaoh: **THE FOURTH LUNTER:** three of his four cards here are lands. This is the one that drains at your end step — and the one the record stopped short of calling a table-kill.
captions.Sanctum Seeker: **PAINTED BY THE COMMANDER'S OWN ARTIST:** Volkan Baǵa made both, and the pair is stack 003 — seven attackers, 14 off each opponent, before blockers.
captions.Savai Triome: **THE SCENERY PAINTER'S TRADE:** a Lunter landscape that fixes all three of Edgar's colours and carries the basic land types Bloodstained Mire and Marsh Flats go looking for.

departments.pull_quote: We count cards, not copies. Four Swamps are one credit.
departments.note: artist-credits reports standout Titus Lunter at 4 entries (4.1% share, runner-up 2) with drop_runs empty; per-entry counting per the department rule, and the concentration caveat from notes[] is honoured in the copy — no invented taste.

rhythm_notes: The Kill closes Act II as the peak; its seven case features read as narrative, so the dense pages sit where the spec puts them. The one dense-dense adjacency, Sources Say into By the Numbers, is covered by the declared full-bleed art break after sources-say. Know Your Enemy (reference) is buffered by What's-adjacent instruction on both sides; Judge's Desk is cushioned by The Short List (imagination) before and Featured Artist (appreciation) after. Low-intensity browsing in The 99 lands right after the two Act I features so the reader gets a breather before the Keep or Ship drill.
gaps: Stacks 002 and 008 cast Gifted Aetherborn, a card not in the 99 — the math holds for any {B}{B} Vampire (Cordial Vampire is the in-deck example), but the scenario boards deserve a touch-up so Judge's Desk never names a card the deck does not run.

Editor-facing context blocks in the extras of stacks 006, 007 and 008 narrate the deck's git history; if the renderer ever prints extras verbatim, they would break the reader's-first rule. Known open issue — needs an artifact-level fix, not a regex.
Stack 004's extras cross-reference stack 001, which is not presentable — a rendered pointer would dangle.

Two lines from the strategic frame still need a stack scenario before they can be stated as fact: the exact drain total when a sweeper resolves through Blood Artist + Cruel Celebrant with Vito on board, and whether Bloodletter of Aclazotz doubles the death drains under an opponent's sweeper (its clause reads 'during your turn'; the matchups prose already declines to extend it).

Strategy DB has no school for death-trigger value engines (aristocrats), typal density, or command-zone engines — three research topics the frame names; the coaching here leans on wrath-math and critical-mass instead.

goldfish_targets' protection group is measured as 'held by turn 6 in 50.0% of games' — half the games have no protection when the wipe lands, which the coach copy handles honestly, but a decision spread on wipe insurance sequencing would make it teachable.
